title: Syllabus
text:
Assessments in brief
Weekly exercises are released after class in Weeks 1–12 and due 11:59 PM the following Tuesday. They are distributed and submitted through GitHub Classroom; an autograder reports which questions pass every time you push, and you may resubmit freely before the deadline. Late: 20% penalty within 24h, 40% within 48h, zero after that.
In-class quizzes (15–20 minutes, five total) are done individually without AI tools during the last part of class.
The final project is an individual analysis of a public-health dataset: a reproducible Quarto report in a GitHub repository, a 5-minute recorded video walkthrough, and an AI-use appendix. Released Week 10, due 11:59 PM December 16. No late submissions.

title: Statistical Programming in R
text:
Wednesdays 2:00–4:40 PM · 70 Washington Sq S (Bobst), Room LL138 · Sep 2 – Dec 9, 2026 (no class Oct 14)
Welcome! This course teaches R programming for the full data-analysis workflow: wrangling, visualization, simulation, and reproducible reporting with Quarto, using public-health data throughout. You will also learn two skills that now define professional statistical programming: managing code with Git and GitHub, and using AI coding assistants responsibly (prompting, verifying, and debugging AI-generated code).
No prior programming or statistics experience is required.

title: Statistical Programming in R
text:
How the course works

Hands-on classes. Every session alternates short live-coding demos with paired exercises, so you write code in every class.
Instant feedback. Weekly exercises are submitted on GitHub and checked automatically: push your work, see which questions pass, revise, and resubmit until the deadline.
AI, embraced and verified. AI tools are allowed on homework and the project (with disclosure), taught explicitly in Week 8, and set aside during short in-class quizzes where your own fluency is certified.
One real project. The course builds to an individual analysis of a public-health dataset: a reproducible Quarto report, a GitHub repo, and a 5-minute video walkthrough.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text: This course treats AI coding assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and similar) as professional tools: you will learn to use them effectively and critically, and you will also develop the individual fluency to program without them.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Why this policy
Statistical programmers now work alongside AI tools daily. Banning them would prepare you for a world that no longer exists; letting them do your thinking would leave you unable to catch their mistakes, and they make plenty. The course therefore teaches the skill that actually matters: directing AI tools and verifying their output. Week 8 is a dedicated workshop, and every week includes a short “AI corner” showing one good and one bad AI use for that week’s topic.
Free-tier AI tools are sufficient for all coursework; no paid subscriptions are required or expected.
Submitting AI-generated work you do not understand, using AI during a quiz, or omitting required disclosure is an academic-integrity violation.

title: Final Project
text:
Note



Full instructions and the grading rubric will be released in Week 10 (November 11). This page summarizes the shape of the project so you can plan ahead.
Each student produces a comprehensive statistical analysis of a public-health dataset, modeled on the Week 10 case study.

title: Final Project
text:
Deliverables (due 11:59 PM, Wednesday December 16)

A GitHub repository containing all code and a reproducible Quarto report with sections on introduction, data preparation, exploratory data analysis (tables, plots, results, interpretations), and summary. The report must render from your repository as submitted.
A 5-minute recorded video walkthrough of your analysis: what question you asked, what you found, and a tour of your key figures.
An AI-use appendix: what you asked AI tools, what they produced, and what you verified or changed.
